utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.5, the Prosecutor versus Baton Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This morning, we will start with the pre-trial conference; and once we are completed with the pre-trial conference, we will start immediately to trial. Could I have the appearances, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues Mr. Vincent Lunny and our case manager, Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. For the Defence, please. Could you please activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Okay. It's Christian Kemperdick for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kemperdick, and I see Mr. Haxhiu is present. I would first like to go through a few matters. There is a motion to amend the indictment, and the Chamber would like to deliver its decision on this motion. As a matter of fact, it is a mixed motion. It is about lifting the confidentiality of the indictment, and it is about an amendment to the indictment. Mr. Kemperdick, I've not heard of any objection against the amendment of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No objection arised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Then I'll deliver the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution motion regarding the indictment. In its order lifting the confidentiality of the indictment, filed on the 20th of May, 2008, the Chamber made public the indictment in this case and redacted the information revealing the date of the publication central to this case, the name of the newspaper, where it was published, and the accused's position with that newspaper at that time. On the 9th of June, 2008, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion seeking that the indictment be made public in its unredacted form. It argues that the details about the publication are already widely known to the public and that under these circumstances, and I quote, "any perceived need to redact that information from the indictment for an abundance of caution no longer exists." In its motion, the Prosecution also requests that the accused's date and place of birth be corrected. In an addendum to the motion, filed on the 11th of June, 2008, the Prosecution requests that the word "willingly" in the first sentence of the unnumbered paragraph on page 2 of the indictment be changed to "wilfully." The Defence has now expressed that it is does not object to the motion. And the Chamber finds that despite the strong likelihood that the information redacted in the mentioned order of 20th of May, 2008, is widely known to the public, or perceived to be known, these proceedings should not further contribute to the dissemination of information which may infringe on the protective measures of a witness who has testified before the Tribunal. Therefore, the Prosecution's request that the indictment be made public in its unredacted form is denied. The requests to correct the accused's date and place of birth and also to change the word "willingly" to "wilfully" in the indictment are granted. The indictment, with those modifications, is from now on the operative indictment in this case. The Prosecution is invited to file the corrected versions of the indictment, in both redacted and unredacted forms, at a later stage for the sake of the record. This concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. Then there is a request to add a document to the Prosecution 65 ter list. The Prosecution wants to add the accused's interview to its exhibit list, and there was objection against adding the exhibit to the list. No further decision at this moment is taken then to add it to the list, and that request is granted. Of course, the usual criteria will be applied if the Prosecution seeks this document, this exhibit to be admitted into evidence. For practical purposes, the Chamber establishes that it has received information from the parties that there will be no need for final briefs in this case. In an informal e-mail exchange of last Friday, the parties implicitly agreed that there should be no final briefs in this case, and it is good to have this on the record. I take it that I summarised the positions of the parties well. Then that is on the record. The OTP filed a submission on the 19th of June in relation to disclosure. There was one important document which was not yet disclosed. I think, at this moment, it suffices to say that the motion is accepted to the extent that the Chamber is now informed about this disclosure. The submission was a submission pursuant to Rule 67(D) in which the Prosecution disclosed an item to the Defence that it had inadvertently failed to disclose to the Defence previously, and the Prosecution asks the Chamber to accept the submission as part of the record, which the Chamber hereby does. It is on my agenda that the Prosecution would call one witness at trial. Mr. Saxon, is that still your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In a pre-trial conference, usually the times available for the parties is set. As was already communicated informally, the Chamber has in its mind that the Prosecution has one hour and fifteen minutes maximum to present its case. That was clear to you already, Mr. Saxon, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would it cause you any problems to do so in one hour and fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will not. That's then on the record. A similar time is granted to the Defence. Mr. Kemperdick, would that cause you any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that both parties have one hour and fifteen minutes maximum to present their cases, including all the bookkeeping matters on exhibits. I also understood, Mr. Kemperdick, that the Defence does not intend to present any oral evidence by witnesses, but that you rely on statements, from what I see, four statements under 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: That is correct; however, it would be five statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five statements. Mr. Saxon, have you received these five statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have received the statements, themselves, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection against introducing this evidence? Of course, we'll do that at trial, but just for us to know, will there be any objections against the introduction of these statements under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, providing, of course, that the Defence has complied with the criteria underneath the Rule, but we expect that has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, at this moment, I've got nothing else on my agenda. There is one matter, however, I would like to briefly raise; that is, this case is a contempt case. It is about the publication of the identity of a protected witness in the Haradinaj case. I suggest to the parties that since there seems to be no need to ever mention this name and to do it in private session, that we'll use the synonym that was granted to that witness in the Haradinaj case, (redacted) that we do not have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, and with the greatest --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, and with the greatest of respect, it had actually been the Prosecution's intention today simply to refer in public session to the witness as "the witness" or "the protected witness," because the Prosecution's concern is that reference to the actual number might facilitate the connection between that pseudonym and testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I find some inconsistency in the previous motion not to further amend the indictment, because that seems to fairly contradict each other. But I'm fine, if we talk about "the witness," we'll all know what witness we are talking about. The Chamber has received a finding shared by the two parties on agreed facts that was filed yesterday. We received them, and during trial we'll say more about that. Then, finally, the Chamber was informed that Mr. Haxhiu would like to make an unsworn statement. Mr. Kemperdick, the Rules give an opportunity to make such a statement either at the beginning of the case, at the start of the case, or delay it until the beginning of the Defence case. Could you inform the Chamber about what you had in mind in view of this unsworn statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had in mind that my client, or Mr. Haxhiu, makes the statement at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the Defence case or of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That request is granted. That means after the opening statements. That's what Rule 84 bis tells us. Is there any matter to be raised during this pre-trial conference? Mr. Saxon, I see you're nodding "no." Mr. Kemperdick is making the same gesture. That means this concludes the pre-trial conference, unless one of my colleagues will have something. No. Then this concludes the pre-trial conference, and we'll proceed immediately to trial. That means that we now start the trial proceedings in the case against Mr. Haxhiu. To start with, Mr. Haxhiu, could you state your full name and date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not receive translation on Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Baton Haxhiu, 24th of February, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not your mistake, Mr. Haxhiu. Please be seated. I'd like to give the opportunity, if there's any need, to make an opening statement. Mr. Saxon, you have an opportunity to do it now. And for the completeness of the record, present at trial, as was the case during the pre-trial conference, is Mr. Saxon for the Prosecution, Mr. Kemperdick for the Defence, and Mr. Haxhiu is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution will not be making an opening statement today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the same applies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same applies to the Defence. So we are now at the stage after the opening statements, and Mr. Haxhiu has been given an opportunity to make an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis. Mr. Haxhiu, I have to inform you that the Trial Chamber will decide on the probative value, if any, of your statement. That means that whatever you say, we can consider to use this as evidence and to consider the probative value. Mr. Haxhiu, you have an opportunity to make a statement under Rule 84 bis, which is an unsworn statement on which you will not be examined by counsel for the Prosecution or for the Defence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judges, honourable Mr. Prosecutor and the Defence counsel, and everybody present here. I shall not be dwelling here on the freedom of expression, and not even on myself and the professionalism with which I tackle my job, but I shall be focusing on the need to build a democratic society in Kosovo. I will not be lecturing here on the importance of the freedom of expression here before you, because we're all part and parcel of democratic societies that have a long consolidated tradition on the freedom of expression and the free media which enjoy the defence of sustainable institutions. But I shall be expressing in my deep conviction that should the citizens be deprived of information of what's happening around them, or, worse, were they to be kept in the dark regarding the development and the activity of their political leaders, their life and their future might be put at peril. And I, therefore, remain deeply convinced that information, regardless of the nature of the news, be it good or bad news, remains essential to the -- to a normal and democratic society. My past experience in Yugoslavia has taught me that weak institutions need inevitably the support of clandestine and illegal activities, which, at the end of the day, do threaten the freedom of an individual and an individual's fundamental freedoms. I am deeply dissatisfied that we have been focusing here, the Prosecutor has been focusing here on the revelation of the identity of the witness, and I want here to stress that the Prosecution side has been trying to use this as a pretext to suggest that the family have been put at some inconvenience. And I will repeat it here that never in my life have I been trying to interfere with the administration of justice when I wrote the article referred to. In particular, let me emphasise here that never did I intend to threaten the witness or his family, and neither did I want to undermine his evidence against -- in the trial and against Ramush Haradinaj. I do fundamentally believe in the mission that The Hague Tribunal has, to bring justice to the former Yugoslavia, and I have tried to convey this to my readers in the course of my job as a journalist. I, alongside my family and friends, I have been a supporter of the view that this Tribunal has been contributing tremendously to the process of reconciliation throughout Yugoslavia and in Kosovo. In my personal capacity, I have been here as a witness twice, and at a time when it could have been potentially threatening to me personally; and even though I was offered protective measures, I decided to give evidence openly. I have and remain committed that it is best for everything that happened during the course of the war in Yugoslavia to be made public, and I've written freely and I abide by the view that citizens need to express their views freely. Honourable Judge, even though I have expressed the deepest regret regarding the interpretation that the Prosecution side has made, as concerns the revelation of the identity of the witness, let me emphasise that even though I wrote that article, the very same witness, using his own name, has previously made, through another newspaper, a number of comments regarding the Kosovo Liberation Army and Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: position of Ramush Haradinaj in his capacity as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll instruct the registrar to make a redaction. You're referring to, and this would -- let's move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the statement being made by the accused here, and can he kindly be asked to slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, could you please slow down your speed of speech, so that the interpreters can translate everything you say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge, Kosovo is a small country where secrets cannot survive for a very long time, especially where they concern people and circumstances surrounding the leaders, certain leaders of the armed forces in Kosovo at the time. At the time of the publication of my article, there were quite a few people who could have been aware of the name of this witness, as well as the fact that he had testified here in the trial of Haradinaj. The subject matter of this article, on which I stand accused in front of you here today, does not constitute a revelation of the name of the witness. The headline of this article has to do with Mr. Haraqija and the fact that they were involved in the publication of the name of this witness. Were the subject of the article be entirely centred on the evidence given against Mr. Haradinaj, this article would have had his name and his evidence, especially at the time when I became acquainted with the name of this witness. As has now been proven, I learned of the identity of this witness about four months before the publication of this article; and had it been my intention to affect the testimony, I would have been able to do this about four months before the publication of the article upon which I stand accused today. However, upon learning of the identity of this witness, I was entirely convinced that his name would not have been -- ought not to have been made public before he were to testify. In addition to that, from June 2007, we knew that he was going to testify against Ramush Haradinaj; and, as a matter of fact, I never considered that to be of vital importance or of journalistic importance, because at the end of the day, this was not news in Kosovo anymore. However, when I learned of the inquiry against Mr. Haraqija and Mr. Morina [as interpreted] - Haraqija was a Minister at the time - and the allegations against this witness, I did consider this to be news of which the public had a vested interest to learn about, and I thought that there was journalistic value and merit in their publication. Let me, in particular, underline that speculation that there was an idea to -- there was an idea that there was an effort to affect the outcome of the evidence comes from the high levels of UNMIK; and, that, in my view, was news. And the article that I've written about spoke about a conspiracy which aimed at affecting the outcome of the evidence of this witness, and which, at the end of the day, had to have an influence on the investigations against Mr. Haraqija and Mirena. At the time, I was convinced that revealing the name of the witness did not constitute a breach of the Rules of Evidence, because this witness had testified against Ramush Haradinaj. In addition, given that Ms. Haraqija and Mirena were under investigation regarding their role in this matter, I thought that the whole affair had become public, and which, in a way, gave me the right to write about it publicly. Your Honour, let me reiterate, once again, that I remain deeply dissatisfied with the view that the Prosecution has that this article constitutes a violation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. Given that I have testified before this Tribunal and I have supported the Prosecution side as well as the Judges, I feel humiliated to be put in this position, given that I wrote the article regarding Mr. Haraqija and Mr. Mirena, because from the highest levels of UNMIK, there was an effort, I thought, about influencing the outcome of the evidence of that witness. And, therefore, I remain deeply convinced that in this whole affair I remain innocent, and I plead here before you to pronounce me innocent in this court of law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhiu. Mr. Saxon, are you ready to present the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Excuse me. There might be one incorrect translation of what Mr. Haxhiu intended to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kemperdick, what he intended to say or what he said might be not the same, first of all, so if you say what he intended to say. If you write down exactly from the transcript which line, which portion it is that you have doubts about, then we'll verify that at a later stage. We have the audio recording of both the original words spoken and, of course, of the translation. We will then verify that. If you will please write it down, "These and these words on that and that lines on the transcript," then we'll take care of it. However, I would try to avoid that you say what he actually intended to say and how it should have been translated, because that might have an effect which is to be avoided. So please write it down and we'll take care of it. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution is ready to proceed, and my colleague, Mr. Lunny, will call the first witness, the only witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lunny, the witness you'd like to call is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The one Prosecution witness to be called this morning is Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I take it you are Mr. Mitford-Burgess. Mr. Mitford-Burgess, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed to you by Madam Usher. I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The record is not complete yet. Yes. Mr. Mitford-Burgess, you will be examined by Mr. Lunny, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Lunny, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I invite both you, Mr. Lunny, and you, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to make a small pause between question and answer, so as to enable the interpreters to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mitford-Burgess.

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to tell the Court your full name and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: My name is Peter John Mitford-Burgess. I am an investigator with the ICTY Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And when you say "investigator," is that with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And how many years have you been employed in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Prior to your employment with the OTP, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I understand you were employed as a police officer in New Zealand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: How many years of police service did you have before coming to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Twenty-nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to the matter in hand, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I understand that in January of this year, you were tasked with investigating an alleged contempt of court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And I further understand you carried out this investigation with a colleague from the OTP, a fellow investigator, Mr. Barry Hogan.

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this investigation was authorised by a decision from the Tribunal dated 16th of January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Under very broad terms, the investigation was related to a newspaper article that published a protected -- sorry, the name of a protected witness from the trial of Haradinaj et al?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, the Prosecution would wish to distribute a series of binders for all parties in the courtroom. It is the intention of the Prosecution to tender a number of exhibits through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From the list we have received, and while waiting for the distribution of the binders, we also see that even the ICTY Rules are on the list of exhibits to be tendered. I don't know whether that is still the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is no longer the case, and Your Honours will see that tab number 1 has been removed, as it is no longer necessary, given discussions between myself, my colleague, and my learned friend Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is an old Latin saying, "jus curia novit," which means "the judge knows the law." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, can I ask you, please, to turn firstly to tab number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny, I take it that you'll pay proper attention to any need to go into private session, if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you recognise this item at tab number 6?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, please, what this item is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: It's an article from a newspaper that was published in Pristina, Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And is it the same newspaper article that was the subject of your investigation for alleged contempt of court?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And if you turn to the back of tab 6, you will see an English translation of the same newspaper article. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this point, may we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session, and the exhibits shown during private session should not be made public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, can you now please look at and turn to tabs 2, 3, 4, and 5. Do you recognise these documents, Mr. Mitford-Burgess?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And, collectively, what are these documents?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: These documents are a series of motions by the Prosecution, and decisions and orders of the Trial Chamber, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And do these motions, decisions, and orders relate to the protective measures for the witness we are discussing here today?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to have tabs 2, 3, 4, and 5 tendered as exhibits, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Registrar, could you assign numbers to 2, 3, 4, and 5 from the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 2, Your Honours, will be assigned P2; tab 3 will be assigned as P3; tab 4 will be assigned Exhibit number P4; and tab 5 will be assigned Exhibit number P5, all under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Kemperdick?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: No objections, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P2, 3, 4, and 5 are admitted into evidence, under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I understand that in the course of your investigations, you and your colleague, Mr. Hogan, interviewed three suspects in relation to this article; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And who were the three suspects you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: The accused, Mr. Baton Haxhiu; Mr. Ilir Mirena, and Mr. Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I understand that all three interviews took place in the Pristina field office of the ICTY; the first two on the 6th of February, and the third one on the 7th of February, 2007. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the interviews were conducted by yourself and Mr. Hogan, with the assistance of an interpreter in each case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, could you please turn with me to tab number 8. And do you recognise this document, Mr. Mitford-Burgess?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court what this document is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: This is an English transcript of the interview that was conducted with the accused, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And was Mr. Haxhiu interviewed as a witness or as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He was interviewed as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in this capacity as a suspect, did you read to Mr. Haxhiu his rights as provided under Rules 42 and 43 of the Rules of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was informed of his rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: During the course of the interview, did Mr. Haxhiu indicate to you that he understood those rights?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Haxhiu waive his right to have a lawyer present for the interview on 6th of February, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to the interview itself, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, are you aware whether or not Mr. Haxhiu, himself, has testified as a witness before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. He has previously testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And do you know when he testified before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He testified as a witness in the Milosevic and Milutinovic cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn to page 7 of the interview and look at lines 7 to 11. During the course of the interview, did Mr. Haxhiu indicate to you that he was aware that some witnesses at the Tribunal testified with protective measures?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to please turn with me to page 22, and can you please look at lines 26 to 30. Did Mr. Haxhiu make any reference, during his interview, to the status of the witness named in his article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And what was the reference to the status of the witness?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He stated that the witness was, in fact, a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you now please turn with me to page 15, line 15 of the interview. Did Mr. Haxhiu make any reference to the Rules of the Tribunal during his interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. In answer to a question, he made the comment, "I was aware of the Tribunal regulations."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, are the Rules of the Tribunal available on the internet in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to turn to page 7. Before I do so, one further question in relation to the Albanian version of the Rules. Where are they available on the internet?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: At the ICTY web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask you to turn, please, to page 7, and look at lines 23 to 27. Did Mr. Haxhiu indicate to you whether he sought any legal advice prior to publishing his article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: In response to the question: "Did you seek legal advice about that," he replied: "No. I didn't speak to a lawyer."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you now turn with me, please, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to page 22, and look at lines numbered 21 to 25. During the interview of Mr. Haxhiu, did Mr. Haxhiu indicate whether he attempted to contact the ICTY for advice before he published his article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: In response to a question, the accused replied: "The only contact I had with the Tribunal was to ask whether the minister would be called by the Tribunal, nothing else."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you now please turn, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to page 21, and look at lines 30 to 32. Did Mr. Haxhiu discuss whether his publication of the article was consistent with the Rules of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: During an answer to a question, he stated: "I broke the Rule of the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution now moves to tender this interview as an exhibit, under seal; and it then recovers the audio CD recording of the interview, together with the Albanian and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the interview of the 6th of February, 2008, audio and transcript in both languages, Albanian and English, would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The CD would be given Exhibit P6, Your Honours; the transcript would be given P6.A; and the transcript in English would be given P6.A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection, Mr. Kemperdick?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Exhibit P6, P6.A, and P6.A.1 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, the next interview you conducted also on the 6th of February, 2008, was of Mr. Ilir Mirena; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the capacity of Mr. Mirena -- or, rather, the employment of Mr. Mirena is he was the editor of the national section of the newspaper in question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And present at the interview was yourself, Mr. Hogan, and the Albanian translator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to tab number 9 in the binder. Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Court what this document is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: This is the English transcript of the interview that was conducted with Mr. Ilir Mirena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And was Mr. Mirena interviewed as a witness or as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He was interviewed as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: At the start of the interview, did you explain to Mr. Mirena his rights under Rules 42 and 43?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. These rights were explained to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And then did Mr. Mirena indicate that he understood those rights?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mirena waive his right to a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to have tab 9 admitted as an exhibit, under seal. And, again, Your Honours, there is an audio CD, an English transcript, and an Albanian transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 9, Your Honours, will be P7; the Albanian transcript will be P7.A; and the English transcript will be Exhibit P7.A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Kemperdick?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Exhibit P7, P7.A, and P7.A.1 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, that the next person you interviewed with Mr. Astrit Haraqija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija was the minister for youth, culture, and sport in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this interview took place the following day also at the Pristina field office on the 7th of February, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And, again, the interview with carried out by yourself, Mr. Hogan, with the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you turn with me, please, to tab number 10 in the binder. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Mitford-Burgess?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what this document is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: This is the English transcript of the interview that was conducted with Mr. Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Haraqija interviewed as a witness or as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He was interviewed as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And did you explain to Mr. Haraqija his rights under Rules 42 and 43?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. These rights were explained to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Haraqija confirm he understood those rights?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Haraqija waive his right to a lawyer for the interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: During the course of the interview, did you show Mr. Haraqija a newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Haraqija recognise the newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, to turn to page 4, line 9, of the interview of Mr. Haraqija. Did Mr. Haraqija say whether or not Mr. Haxhiu contacted him prior to the publication of the article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. In response to a question, he stated: "Baton called me."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you also to look at page 4, still on page 4, and look at lines 25 to 27. During the course of Mr. Haraqija's interview, did Mr. Haraqija provide any particular information about the conversation he had with Mr. Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, in part, "I told him I was under investigation for intimidating a protected witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution now moves to tender tab 10 as an exhibit, under seal. And, again, Your Honours, there is an audio CD, an English transcript, and an Albanian transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 10, Your Honours, will be assigned Exhibit P8; with the Albanian transcription as P8.A; and the English transcription as P8.A.1, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Exhibit P8, P8.A, and P8.A.1 are admitted into evidence, under seal. To the extent I may have forgotten for the previous exhibit, to say that when the registrar indicated it was admitted under seal, that it was also admitted under seal. This one as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, changing topics, to your knowledge, following Mr. Haxhiu's initial appearance at the Tribunal, did the Chamber grant his request for provisional release?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you know and recall what conditions, if any, were placed on Mr. Haxhiu's provisional release?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I believe that he was required not to discuss the case publicly or with the media, with the exception of his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I would now wish to show you part of a video. If you could watch this, I'll ask you a number of questions after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, Your Honours, this is a first segment of item number 12 in the Prosecution's 65 ter list, and runs from eight seconds to fifty seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I do not know what the content of the video is. Is there any need to go into private session or to have it not being shown to the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The video can be shown in public session, and it relates to the motions previously filed by the Prosecution in relation to an interview given by Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Good evening, honoured viewers. We are broadcasting live from an improvised studio for the television programme 'Opinion Plus' in Hotel Grand Pristina. "This is a live interview with the journalist Baton Haxhiu, well-known personality for the television programme 'Opinion,' and the views of the 'Opinion Plus.' He has been focused on the media during these past two weeks since his indictment from the OTP, and after he was handed over to The Hague with regard to the disclosure of one of the witness's name in the case against former Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj. "It was, indeed, a story which drew the attention of many in Albania and which bore solidarity in the media and beyond. "Mr. Haxhiu, good evening, and thank you for coming here."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you recognise that video sample --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you recognise the piece of video you've just been shown?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what this video shows?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: It records an interview conducted by an Albanian television journalist with the accused, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you know when this interview was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, not the specific date. I believe it was probably earlier this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness now to be shown a second excerpt from the video, which runs from one minute 58 seconds to three minutes 38 seconds. And for the benefit of Your Honours and my learned friend, the transcript of the interview in question, the relevant pages are pages 3 to 5, Your Honours, starting just below halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Starting from the start, when did this question start? When did you become aware that there was an indictment against you? "I learned of the case around January of this year. Question: "Did it start this year in January, when The Hague was proceeding against you? "No. I received information that I had to go to an informative meeting with the so-called investigators of the ICTY, with whom -- who later informed me about an article published in the "Disemblastija" [phoen]. Question: "How did you receive the information? How does this procedure operation, or is this a secret? Answer: "According to the procedure, they send a letter, and the letter arrived in my office, and they invite you for an informative conversation. Question: "Does this take place in The Hague or in Pristina? Answer: "It's in the Tribunal's office in Pristina. Question: "In Pristina. And this conversation took place sometime in January? Haxhiu: "Yes, around January. Question: "And they informed that you're being indicted? Haxhiu: "No, no. I was interviewed regarding the article and the publication procedure. That was all. But I didn't believe that an indictment could be issued against me. Question: "Why did they issue the indictment, and when were you informed about it? Haxhiu: "I cannot talk about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, only a moment. There seems to be two lines missing from the end of that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny, what do you exactly mean by "two lines missing"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it had been the intention of the Prosecution to stop the clip midway down page 5, finishing with the word "travelled."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then play the relevant part again, but perhaps especially those parts that are missing, perhaps not the whole portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be a technical problem with the sound at this point. If Your Honours would please bear with me, as we attempt to correct that difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, does it mean that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It was an information conversation which takes place in the offices of the ICTY in Pristina. Question: "And the conversation was around January?" Answer: "Yes." "And did they tell you that you were indicted? "Answer: "No, no. I was interviewed regarding the article and the publication procedure. That was all. But I didn't believe an indictment could be issued against me. Question: "Why did they issue an indictment, and when were you informed about it?" Haxhiu: "I cannot talk about this." Question: "But when were you informed that there was issued an indictment against you? Answer: "One day, 24 hours before I travelled: "How did the information reach you? Answer: "It's simple, since the UNMIK and the Kosovo police took into account the fact ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you recognise that excerpt of the video?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Is that from the same interview of Mr. Haxhiu on Kosovo TV?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you know which television station broadcast the interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I believe it was TV Klan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And I show you a third and final excerpt from the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this can be found at page 33 of the English transcript and running to page 35, and the time code for the video is 38 minutes and 37 seconds, to 40 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In fact, why were you indicted? Who is this person, the name of which you've revealed? "I have already violated Article 77. "What is this article? "I said that I've violated Article 77 of the Tribunal. I've published something that shouldn't have been published. "Were you aware of Article 77? I think that -- I'm just asking because I wonder how could you violate a rule if you weren't aware of it? "If possible, I would have loved to be able to stay in Pristina and Kosovo from sometime until the trial begins. "Why would a journalist have to comply with The Hague Rules, Mr. Haxhiu? It's The Hague, itself, that should safeguard the secrets, not journalists. Haxhiu: "First of all, I shouldn't have a citizen of Kosovo and have an UNMIK United Nations missive Kosovo passport. Had I been in possession of an Albanian passport, Albania is outside The Hague Tribunal's jurisdiction. Question: "But are you also an Albanian citizen? Aren't you also an Albanian citizen; right? Haxhiu: "I didn't use that one because, only later, did I learn from Sokol Lako that if you were a citizen of Albania. Question: "The Hague has no right. Haxhiu: "The Hague has no right. Question: "But you're not under its jurisdiction, and we could have published the same name many times and not have had the same fate as yours. Haxhiu: "Correct. Bushati got away with it. He mentioned the name, and he got away with it. Question: "And when were you released?" Haxhiu: "When I was released, the most horrifying thing was, again, the handcuffing. Question: "So you were again handcuffed during your release? Haxhiu: "After the airport."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, do you also recognise this excerpt as being from the TV Klan interview of Mr. Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution now moves to tender tab 12, the added tab on its 65 ter list, as a public exhibit in this trial; that is, the DVD showing the video interview itself, together with the English and Albanian transcripts of the interview. And for the purposes of the record, again, I would state for the benefit of the record that the first excerpt runs from eight seconds to fifty seconds and can be found in page 1 of the transcripts; the second excerpt is one minute 58 seconds to three minutes and 38 seconds, running from page 3 to page 5; and, finally, the third excerpt from 38 minutes and 37 seconds to 40 minutes and 2 seconds, being at pages 33 to page 35 of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you want to tender the whole of the interview, although you mentioned the portions played in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I do object to having tab 12 admitted and tendered. I don't think it has any bearing on the case, to be quite honest. Mr. Haxhiu stands accused for his conduct with the Tribunal, and the interview was conducted after the alleged article was written. So I don't really see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny, relevance has been raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the Klan TV interview serves two purposes which would merit this submission under Rule 98 on account of its probative value. And, firstly, the Prosecution would stress that as the article shows at the first page of the transcript, this interview was conducted within two weeks of Mr. Haxhiu's first appearance at the Tribunal; his initial appearance, rather, when he was imposed with a number of special conditions of provisional release, including a condition that he not speak to the media. And yet despite that, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the condition, that he not speak to the media?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and not to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in general terms not to speak to the media?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Not to speak to the media about his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About his case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And I submit that the excerpt shown demonstrates that he did, indeed, speak about the case, and in particular the last, the third portion played talks about the allegation of violation of Article 77 of the Tribunal. He talks about The Hague should safeguard the secrets of witnesses, not journalists. And in particular, that comment about the journalists being the ones to protect -- rather, The Hague is the body to protect witnesses, not journalists, is indicative of Mr. Haxhiu's state of mind. It indicates his understanding of the Rules, his reckless disregard for the Rules. It shows his indifference to what he was told two weeks earlier, not to discuss his case with the public. And despite that, in a very short space of time, he does exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's about attitude of this accused; is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. And, secondly, Your Honours, it would also be, in our view, or at least the submission of the Prosecution, a matter relevant to sentencing, again given his attitude shortly after being imposed with special conditions of provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kemperdick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I maintain my position and objection. Mr. Haxhiu in the interview, on several occasions, says, "I cannot talk about this, I cannot talk about this. In fact, I cannot talk about this. I may not talk. I may talk about everything but the case related to which I am indicted." The journalist persists and keeps asking him, but he keeps telling him, "I cannot talk about this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEMPERDICK
utterances.text: One more thing, Your Honour, please. He's indicted for violation of Rule 77. That is public.
